curriculum.lesson_evidence: Our bodies give us early warning signs when something feels unsafe, such as a fast heartbeat, a tight tummy, sweaty hands or wanting to run away. A situation can be safe, unsafe or unsure. If it is unsafe or unsure we can say 'No' or 'Stop', go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult, and keep telling until someone listens. Our bodies belong to us, and nobody should hurt us or ask us to keep a secret that makes us feel worried or unsafe.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
An older child says, 'Don't tell anyone, it's our secret,' about something that made you worried. Is this safe, unsafe or unsure, and what should you do?

FEEDBACK
Unsafe or unsure: a secret that makes you worried should be told. Say 'No', go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult. A happy surprise that will soon be shared is different from a secret that worries you.

WATCH FOR
Thinking you will get in trouble for telling. Trusted adults want to know, and telling keeps people safe.

INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE

Write a short reflection naming one choice you changed and why. Any movement is optional, adult-supervised and can be done in a gentler way or described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: a stranger offers Sam a lift home. Early warning signs: his tummy feels tight and he feels nervous. Situation: unsafe. Action: say 'No thanks', walk to a safe place such as the shop or a teacher and tell a trusted adult. A safe situation: a family member collects him at the usual place.

TRY FIRST
An older child says, 'Don't tell anyone, it's our secret,' about something that made you worried. Is this safe, unsafe or unsure, and what should you do?

FEEDBACK
Unsafe or unsure: a secret that makes you worried should be told. Say 'No', go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult. A happy surprise that will soon be shared is different from a secret that worries you.
teach_steps.explain:
Our bodies give us early warning signs when something feels unsafe, such as a fast heartbeat, a tight tummy, sweaty hands or wanting to run away. A situation can be safe, unsafe or unsure. If it is unsafe or unsure we can say 'No' or 'Stop', go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult, and keep telling until someone listens. Our bodies belong to us, and nobody should hurt us or ask us to keep a secret that makes us feel worried or unsafe.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the cues, rules or choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For any movement, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby, move at your own comfortable level and stop if anything hurts or feels unsafe. You may always choose a gentler version or only describe the movement. One deliberate, reasoned change is more useful than a longer answer.
